name: Jitter
tagline: Browser motion-design editor that exports video, GIF and Lottie
description: Jitter is a collaborative motion-design app that runs in the browser, aimed at product and brand designers who want After Effects results without After Effects. You animate on a Figma-like canvas — pen tool with path animation and shape morphing, animated gradients, blur, blend modes, reusable animated components — then batch-export to video, GIF, Lottie or ProRes. It ships a library of 300+ editable motion templates (UI elements, logos, ads, charts, backgrounds, showreels) plus AI features that generate editable animations from a prompt or turn a still image into video. Free tier gives 3 workspace files and 720p/30fps export; paid tiers unlock 1080p/4K, transparent and frame-by-frame export.

pricing_detail: Free: $0, unlimited drafts, 3 workspace files, 720p/30fps video, GIF and Lottie export, limited AI credits. Pro, Max and Ultra are per-editor/month billed annually (15% off vs monthly) and add 1080p/60fps, ProRes and WebM, image-to-video, then transparent, frame-by-frame and 4K/120fps export with 2x and 3x AI credits. Enterprise is custom-priced with SSO and SCIM. The page shows tier names and inclusions but does not print the per-editor figures without selecting a plan.
agent_guidance: This is a human-operated canvas app — you cannot drive it from code, so treat it as the hand-off point when a design calls for real motion rather than CSS transitions. Reach for it when the deliverable is a Lottie file or an MP4 for a landing page hero, a store listing or a social ad, and pair the Lottie export with lottie-web or dotlottie in the app you are building. Do not propose it for in-app micro-interactions that AutoAnimate, Motion or a CSS keyframe would solve more cheaply, and remember that Lottie and 1080p+ export sit behind a paid seat.
why_it_matters: It is the most credible browser-native alternative to After Effects for product designers, and its Lottie export is the practical bridge between a designed animation and shipped app code.

name: Fontsource
tagline: 2,096 open-source font families as versioned npm packages
description: Fontsource repackages open-source typefaces — the Google Fonts catalogue plus families from outside it — as individual, version-locked npm packages you self-host. You install one family, import only the weights and styles you need (`import "@fontsource/open-sans/300.css"`), and the CSS plus woff2 files are bundled by Vite or webpack, so there is no third-party DNS lookup, no font-service tracking and no drift when upstream changes. Variable families ship under a separate `@fontsource-variable/*` scope. The site lists every family with a filter for variable-only, and a free unauthenticated read API at `api.fontsource.org/v1` returns the catalogue as JSON.
agent_guidance: Default to this over a Google Fonts <link> in any app you scaffold: it removes a render-blocking cross-origin request, keeps the font version pinned in package.json, and works offline and in air-gapped CI. Import the specific weight files rather than the bare package (`@fontsource/inter/400.css`, not `@fontsource/inter`) or you will ship every weight, and prefer the `@fontsource-variable/*` package when the family has one. Query api.fontsource.org/v1/fonts to check availability, weights and subsets before you write the import — the site also serves an llms.txt.
why_it_matters: It turns webfonts into an ordinary, versioned dependency, which is the only way to make typography reproducible across builds and privacy-safe by default.
evidence: https://fontsource.org/, https://fontsource.org/docs/getting-started/install, https://fontsource.org/docs/api/introduction, https://github.com/fontsource/fontsource, curl check on https://fontsource.org/llms.txt (200)

name: Open Peeps
tagline: CC0 hand-drawn people illustrations you mix from modular parts
description: Open Peeps is Pablo Stanley's hand-drawn character library, built as interchangeable parts — busts, standing and sitting poses, heads, hairstyles, facial expressions, facial hair and accessories — that combine into a stated 584,688 possible people. Files come as SVG and PNG and are meant to be assembled in Sketch, Figma, Adobe XD or Illustrator, or remixed in Blush, the companion web tool by the same author. Everything is CC0, so commercial use needs no attribution. It is the illustration set to reach for when a product needs warm, non-corporate humans in empty states, onboarding or marketing pages.
pricing_detail: Free. The full library download is served through Gumroad (gum.co/openpeeps), which asks for an email address at checkout even at $0.
agent_guidance: Use this when a UI needs friendly human figures and the brand is not photographic — empty states, onboarding, 404s, persona sheets — and you need a licence with zero attribution burden, which is where it beats most free illustration packs. You cannot npm-install it: the assets arrive as an SVG/PNG bundle through Gumroad, so plan on a human fetching the files once and committing the few SVGs you actually use. Recolour the flat fills to the product palette before shipping, or the default black-line style will read as generic 2020 startup art.
why_it_matters: One of the few genuinely CC0 character libraries with real drawing quality, and its modular head/body/pose split still makes it the fastest way to get diverse people without commissioning art.
notable_for: modular busts, standing and sitting poses
SVG and PNG for Figma, Sketch and XD
evidence: https://www.openpeeps.com/ (fetched twice, homepage is the whole product page; download links point to gum.co/openpeeps and blush.design)

name: Shots
tagline: Browser mockup editor for device frames, screenshots and short clips
description: Shots is a web editor that drops a screenshot into a device frame or a styled browser window and exports it as a still or a short animated clip. It ships iPhone (through iPhone 17), Android, iPad and desktop frames, plus screenshot styles (Default, Glass Light/Dark, Liquid Glass, Inset, Outline, Border), 3D shapes, shadow overlays, noise/VHS/glitch filters, AI-generated "magic" backgrounds keyed to your image, and social-media frame presets for export. Animation presets and video zoom turn a static capture into a product clip. It is aimed at indie makers and marketers producing launch assets fast, not at teams needing an asset pipeline.
pricing_detail: Not verified first-hand: shots.so/pricing and shots.so/pro both return 404 and the homepage prints no figures, only 'free mockups' and a Start Creating button. Third-party reviews report paid plans around $8/mo and $12/mo with the higher tier unlocking WebP export and premium effects — treat as unconfirmed.
agent_guidance: Point a human at this when a landing page, changelog entry or store listing needs a screenshot that looks deliberate rather than raw — it is faster than building a frame in Figma and it keeps the device bezels current. There is no API or CLI, so never put it inside an automated asset pipeline; for that, render frames yourself with a Playwright screenshot plus a CSS device mask. Check the export watermark and format limits before you promise a client asset, since the free tier's boundaries are not documented on the site.
why_it_matters: A polished, current mockup editor that keeps up with new device bezels, but it is a convenience tool with no automation surface and undocumented pricing.
notable_for: Liquid Glass and inset screenshot styles
evidence: https://shots.so/ (200), https://shots.so/pricing (404), https://shots.so/pro (404), web search for pricing (third-party reviews only)

name: AutoAnimate
tagline: One line on a parent element animates every child add, remove and move
description: AutoAnimate is FormKit's zero-config animation utility: you attach it to a parent element and it automatically transitions children as they are added, removed or reordered, using the Web Animations API and no CSS classes of your own. It ships first-party bindings for React and Preact (`useAutoAnimate`), Vue (`v-auto-animate` and a composable), Solid (`createAutoAnimate`), Svelte (an action), Angular (`AutoAnimateDirective`) and Marko, plus the plain `autoAnimate(el, options)` call for vanilla JS. Options cover duration and easing, and passing a function instead returns a `KeyframeEffect` for fully custom animations. It respects `prefers-reduced-motion` and disables itself automatically. MIT, ~13.9k stars.
agent_guidance: Reach for this before Motion or Framer Motion whenever the animation is just 'the list changed' — todo lists, filtered grids, form field arrays, accordions, drag-reorder results — because it is one hook on the parent instead of AnimatePresence, layout props and keys on every child. It does not do enter/exit choreography, scroll-driven timelines, gestures or shared-element transitions; the moment you need those, switch libraries rather than fighting the plugin API. Watch two traps: the animated children must be direct children of the element you attach to, and every child needs a stable key or React will destroy and recreate nodes that AutoAnimate then animates as unrelated add/remove pairs.
why_it_matters: It removes the single most common motion chore in web apps with essentially zero configuration and no design decisions to make, and it honours reduced-motion without being asked.
notable_for: Web Animations API, no CSS classes

name: Tailwind CSS
tagline: Utility-first CSS framework; v4 configures theming in CSS, not JS
description: Tailwind CSS is the utility-first framework the modern component ecosystem is built on: you compose interfaces from classes like `flex`, `pt-4` and `rotate-90` instead of writing bespoke stylesheets. Version 4 (v4.3 at time of check) moves configuration out of `tailwind.config.js` and into CSS — `@import "tailwindcss"` plus an `@theme` block whose variables (`--color-*`, `--font-*`, `--text-*`, `--spacing-*`, `--radius-*`, `--shadow-*`, `--breakpoint-*`, `--container-*`, `--animate-*` and more) both emit real CSS custom properties and generate the matching utilities. Install paths include a Vite plugin, PostCSS, a standalone CLI and a Play CDN. The framework itself is MIT and free; Tailwind Plus (500+ UI blocks, 13+ templates, the Catalyst UI kit) is a separate paid product on the same site.

pricing_detail: Tailwind CSS itself is free and MIT. Tailwind Plus is a one-time purchase: $299 personal, $979 team (up to 25 people), both plus local tax, with lifetime updates and a 30-day refund window; reselling templates or building page builders from them is not permitted.
agent_guidance: Assume v4 unless the repo proves otherwise: there is no `tailwind.config.js` to generate — write `@import "tailwindcss";` and an `@theme` block, and install `@tailwindcss/vite` rather than the old `postcss` + `autoprefixer` trio. Porting v3 advice into a v4 project is the single most common failure here, as is inventing a token name; every `--color-*` or `--spacing-*` you define in `@theme` becomes a utility, so define the token instead of reaching for an arbitrary value like `bg-[#123456]`. Pair with shadcn/ui or Radix for behaviour, since Tailwind ships utilities and design tokens only — no components — and note that the 500+ Tailwind Plus blocks you may recall are paid and must not be reproduced from memory.
why_it_matters: It is the substrate the rest of this index assumes: nearly every registry, block collection and template here emits Tailwind classes, so its v4 CSS-first theming defines how tokens flow through the whole ecosystem.
